newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. businessman arrested in S.Korea for spying.
newsitem.headline: U.S. businessman arrested in S.Korea for spying.

text.p: South Korea's top intelligence agency said on Wednesday it had arrested an American businessman for spying.

A spokesman for the Agency for National Security Planning said Donald Ratcliffe, 62, whom it identified as a director in charge of Asian operations at U.S.-based Litton Guidance and Controls Systems, was suspected of collecting military secrets in South Korea.
"The American was arrested today for collecting military secrets here," the official told Reuters, but declined to give details.
But the Dong-A Ilbo newspaper said in its Thursday edition seen on Wednesday that Ratcliffe was suspected of having collected information on Seoul's arms procurements.
The Chosun Ilbo said in its Thursday edition that Ratcliffe was a former U.S. military officer and he was emerging from a U.S. military camp in Seoul when he was arrested.
South Korea is a close ally of the United States, which stations 36,450 troops in South Korea to protect against threats from communist North Korea.
A U.S. embassy spokesman said he had no information on the case. The U.S. military spokesman in South Korea was not immediately available for comment.
No one was available for comment at Litton Industries in California.
South Korea plans to buy arms and military equipment worth billions of dollars by the early 21st century to modernise its defences.
The United States, which Seoul has looked to as a main supplier of military hardware, is now competing with European and Russian suppliers to win more of the planned arms supply contracts.

Earlier on Wednesday the U.S. military denied a Chosun Ilbo report that Ratcliffe had been hiding at a major U.S. military camp in Seoul. The report also said U.S. military officials refused to hand him over to South Korean authorities.
"That part of the article is an absolute lie. We have been coordinating very closely with the Seoul Prosecutor's Office," the U.S. military said in a statement.
"There has been no request to the USFK (U.S. Forces Korea) for assistance. We will, as always, cooperate with the ROK (Republic of Korea) authorities," it said.
Last September U.S. prosecutors arrested Robert Kim, a Korean-born U.S. citizen, on charges of passing more than 40 classified documents to a South Korean embassy official.
One week later a U.S. district judge ordered that Kim be kept in jail pending his trial, overturning an earlier ruling by a magistrate that he be released on a $200,000 bond.
Kim, 56, was a U.S. Navy computer specialist who became a U.S. citizen in 1974.
